 Whiting column: Inflation stems from multiple economic factors
 Opinion Opinion | Oct 23, 2026 
 Bryan Whiting
Personal Responsibility

 Bryan Whiting 
 Economics is simple, complex and evolves over time. Most often logical, but aspects exist beyond the obvious. Recently, proven economic principles are often manipulated by political agendas, making understanding more difficult. Economic reality, however, is unaffected.
 Numerous elements occupy economics: inflation, job opportunities, wage levels, tax rates, costs of production, return on investment, exports and imports, or laws and regulations. Our attention fluctuates, moving toward the aspect currently most affecting us and our system.
 Inflation occupies that position today. Increased prices are not the cause of inflation; they are a symptom. Because inflation is multifaceted, its cause is never singular. Short- and long-term factors are numerous and often not apparent to the naked eye. Understanding the factors precipitating inflation is necessary if we are to control it.
 Devaluation of our currency is one. Devaluation is a function of money supply, its relationship to productivity and its interactions with the supply and demand of goods and services. In simplest terms, economics is the movement of money. Economy is the system a country, society or individual uses to facilitate and govern movement of money in acquiring the available goods and services. The more money moves, the better. Movement facilitates increased transactions, enabling an individual dollar to be utilized multiple times without increasing the money supply.
 Fred has $50. He buys a shirt with the $50. The clothing store pays an employee $50. The employee takes his wife out to a $50 dinner. The restaurant pays the food wholesaler $50 for tomatoes used in salads; the wholesaler pays a farmer $50 for produce; the farmer pays $50 for fertilizer and on and on. The singular $50 is multiplied many times, instead of another $50 being required for each transaction, which would increase the money supply, devaluing the dollar.

 Because the purchased items are used up, consumed, they will need to be repurchased, creating more transactions. This transactional multiplication continues indefinitely until the $50 is utilized for something that isn’t consumed, in effect becoming stuck in that item until replaced or resold; think furniture in the short term or a piece of art in the longer term. Every transaction facilitates increased commerce through additional employees, production, sales and governmental tax revenue.
 Current efforts to completely replace cash with credit and debit card transactions would be detrimental to this transaction multiplier and hence our economy. Transactions would still occur, but issues arise in the protocol. Banks processing transactions charge a 1.5% to 2.5% fee. As a result, in our example, there is only 49 (50 minus $1, or 2%) available for the next transaction. This second transaction will lose 2% as well, reducing the amount available for the next transaction. With enough transactions, the $50 would completely disappear.
 If the government bypasses banks and issues a card containing our funds, processing costs still exist, probably more than the private bank’s 2%. More significantly, the government would know our income sources, tracking and controlling where, when and what we buy.
 Foreign transactions don’t help. Dollars leaving the country negatively affect the transaction multiplier because the “$50” is no longer available. Whether the dollar leaves for a consumer item (toy, car, oil), our vacation in a foreign country or a U.S. resident sending money to a relative in a foreign country, the result is an economic negative.
 Inflationary effects of supply and demand fluctuations are obvious. Supply goes down, price goes up; demand goes up, price goes up, and vice versa in both situations. Supply and demand always win. Solutions are obvious, simple and 100% effective: increase supply and decrease demand. Sometimes, however, political considerations and agendas become a roadblock preventing a solution. Supply and demand are unemotional, which requires us to take the emotion out of decision-making if we’re to develop and implement effective solutions.
 Devaluation occurs when more money is chasing the same amount of groceries, clothing, televisions, plumbers and painters. Prices increase. Each dollar buys less. Consequently, a simple increase in wages causes inflation unless it’s a function of a commensurate increase in productivity. Raises based upon seniority are inflationary; ones based on merit (increased productivity) are not.
 Increasing minimum wage is a catch-22. Those receiving minimum wage could use the increase, but it only helps in the short term because it’s inflationary. All those receiving the raise haven’t increased productivity. Minimum wage increases facilitate big companies getting bigger. Small businesses can’t afford the increase, resulting in lost employees or bankruptcy. Big companies initially absorb the increase, knowing the decreased competition means they can soon raise prices because our demand is still present.
 The government and Fed can increase money supply. In 2010, our money supply (M1) was $1.8 trillion. It became $4 trillion by 2019. Between 2020 and 2022, M1 grew to $20.1 trillion. Because these large increases were not a function of productivity, we are experiencing the resultant inflation. Current M1 is $19.8 trillion. If Trump does give everyone $5,000 after the midterm election, the Fed must increase money supply by $1.2 trillion; inflationary. Any year the national debt increases necessitates an increase in money supply, guaranteeing an inflationary consequence.
 Money received from any government benefit program is inflationary. It doesn’t matter the reason for the program; money supply is increased without an increase in productivity. That would include forgiving student debt. Some programs facilitate a decrease in productivity when someone stops working upon reaching the maximum income eligibility threshold: SNAP, Medicaid, among others. It should be recognized, however, that for some, receiving the aid could enable and facilitate an increase in future productivity.
 All economic decisions and some current events change prices if supply and demand are affected. Nothing is exempt. It can be very straightforward. Total immigration was 11 million from 2020-2025. In 2025, 50 million foreign-born individuals resided in the U.S. Source doesn’t matter: legal, illegal, employed or student. Whether we feel it’s good or bad, immigration increases demand for goods and services, requiring food, education, medical care, transportation, utilities and a place to live. It’s a hard truth, but we can’t be surprised apartment rents or home prices increased dramatically with 11 million additional people combined with the double whammy of increased money supply. Not providing these services but allowing unfettered immigration would be like refusing to buy more hay after buying 10 more horses.
 Some factors are less obvious. Exports are economically positive, but we must realize they increase money supply. The country buys our products with its currency, which isn’t dollars. We immediately convert its money to dollars at the current exchange rate and place it in our banking system. This increases money supply; inflationary.
 All factors combine to produce a current level of inflation; it’s never one factor. Strategies to minimize each are obvious and immediately emerge as we become aware of each. Additional less obvious factors, but no less impactful, will be discussed in the next column. It’s our personal responsibility to understand them and legislatively advocate for the adoption of strategies controlling inflation.
 Bryan Whiting feels most of our issues are best solved by personal responsibility and an understanding of nonpartisan economics rather than government intervention. Comments and column suggestions can be sent to bwpersonalresponsibility@gmail.com .
